archetype.name: Fringe Contender (pass-first, leaky defense)
archetype.definition: A first-year-coach team whose Cousins-led passing attack is good enough to keep it in the wild-card conversation, but whose defense and dead run game leave it as a .500 club until one of them changes.

report.headline: Cousins has the passing game humming; the defense is giving it all back.
report.take:
This is a different franchise than the one that scored 14.2 points a game last year, the worst mark in the league. Under Klint Kubiak, with Kirk Cousins starting every week, the Raiders score 27 a game, sixth-best. The 3-3 record and the exact 162-162 split tell you what they are: a team that trades scores. The point differential implies 2.3 wins, so the record isn't running ahead of the play, and the Book has consistently underrated them. They have covered at a league-best .833 clip.

The offense is entirely the passing game. Pass EPA per play of 0.204 ranks fifth, and Cousins' passing EPA has climbed almost every week, from 0.4 in the opener to 11.5 against Buffalo. The protection supports it: a 3.4% sack rate, third-best, even though pressure gets home more often than you'd like. The run game is the opposite. Rushing EPA ranks 29th and run success rate ranks last, and the line is the cause rather than Ashton Jeanty. Backs average 1.4 yards before contact, the worst figure in the league, and the stuff rate ranks 30th. Jeanty's 36 targets out of the backfield are partly the offense getting him the ball where the line can't fail him. Brock Bowers drew 43 targets in just four games and is the passing game's center of gravity.

The defense is where the record is really decided, and its numbers hide a split. Its pressure rate of 30.3% is third-best and its 10 takeaways rank third. Those takeaways came almost entirely in the first three weeks, against Miami, the Chargers and New Orleans. Two of those offenses rank in the bottom four today. Against KC, New England and Buffalo, the takeaways dried up, and an underlying problem showed: pass EPA allowed ranks 25th, EPA on short passes allowed ranks dead last, missed tackles rank 25th and red-zone touchdown rate allowed ranks 26th. Quarterbacks beat the rush with quick throws, and the yards after the catch pile up. New England threw for 374 in the 45-17 blowout. A defense that depends on turnovers rather than snap-to-snap stops is the most fragile thing on this roster.

Going forward, the schedule changes shape. The remaining slate is heavy on good defenses: Seattle, San Francisco, KC, Denver twice, Cleveland and the Chargers all rank 11th or better on that side. Many of those same teams have bottom-eight offenses. Expect fewer shootouts. The offense will be tested, and the defense should look better than it has. A .500-ish finish with a puncher's chance at a wild card is the honest read, and a big step for a franchise coming off a 3-14 season.

strengths.title: Cousins' passing game is top-five
strengths.body: The Raiders are among the most efficient passing offenses in the league, and the per-game passing EPA has risen almost steadily across six starts. Cousins gets the ball out with good protection against sacks, and Bowers and Jeanty give him reliable underneath targets. This looks sustainable, because it held up against KC and Buffalo, not just the soft early slate.

strengths.title: Protection limits sacks
strengths.body: Only eight sacks allowed, and a sack rate that ranks third, keep drives alive even though pressure arrives at a middling rate. Some of that is Cousins' processing and release. It is a quarterback-driven strength more than a line-driven one, which makes it durable as long as he's upright.

strengths.title: A pass rush that gets home
strengths.body: A 30.3% pressure rate and a QB hit rate that ranks fourth give this defense a real weapon. It is what produced the early-season turnover flurry. The pressure is real. The takeaways it produced are the part to expect less of.

concerns.title: Short passes and tackling get exploited
concerns.body: The defense allows the most EPA in the league on short throws and misses too many tackles. That is how good offenses neutralize the pass rush: get it out quick and let receivers run. Combined with a bad red-zone rate, it explains why points allowed have climbed even as the rush stays strong. It is a structural flaw, not noise.

concerns.title: The run game has no floor
concerns.body: Last in run success and last in yards before contact, the ground game is a line problem that leaves Jeanty getting hit almost at the handoff. It makes the offense one-dimensional and hurts it in short yardage. Nothing in the first six weeks suggests a fix is coming.

concerns.title: Takeaways were front-loaded
concerns.body: The league-top-three takeaway count was built almost entirely in the first three games against weak offenses. Since then there has been one takeaway across three losses. A defense this porous on a per-play basis needs those swings, and they tend to regress.

trend.note: The Raiders won their first three against soft opposition and have lost the three since. The passing EPA has climbed nearly every week, while points allowed have risen from 13 and 14 to 30, 45 and 33. Two of those losses were by three points to KC and Buffalo, and both were covers.

nextGame.headline: A battered Rams front meets Cousins, but McVay's offense finds holes.
nextGame.body:
The Rams come in at 2-4 but are better than that. Their net EPA ranks ninth, and only one team has fewer wins relative to its point differential. Their offense moves the ball at a top-three yardage rate behind a line that allows the lowest pressure rate in the league. That is the worst possible matchup for a Raiders defense that wins with pressure and loses on short passes. On the other side, the Rams' pass defense is elite deep and has been the stingiest in football against tight ends. That is aimed straight at Bowers and Michael Mayer. The Book has the Rams by 4.5 in Las Vegas, with a 47.5 total, indoors.

Availability tilts toward the Raiders. The Rams lost DE Kobie Turner, DT Poona Ford and K Blake Grupe in last week's 18-16 loss to Arizona. Myles Garrett remains on IR, CB Trent McDuffie was inactive last week, and WR Davante Adams is out with a ruptured hamstring. That guts a pass rush that already ranks 21st in pressure. It also hands the kicking job to a replacement on the league's worst special-teams unit. The Raiders lose DT Tonka Hemingway, a rotational interior player at 52% of snaps, to a concussion. TE Carter Runyon and WR Dont'e Thornton Jr. remain on IR, but neither has played this year.

waysToWin.title: Cousins carves a gutted pass rush
waysToWin.body: With Turner, Ford and Garrett out, the Rams' already-modest pressure rate should drop further. Cousins gets clean pockets to work the intermediate middle. If the Rams' deep coverage takes away the shot plays, the Raiders can still march with timing throws, especially to the third receiver, where the Rams have been vulnerable.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage
waysToWin.body: The Rams' special teams already cost them more per game than any team in the league, and now a replacement kicker takes over. Field position, missed kicks and a fourth-quarter field goal that doesn't go in are a realistic path in a game expected to be close.

waysToWin.title: A turnover or two flips it
waysToWin.body: The Raiders' rush still generates hits, and the Rams sit on the wrong side of the turnover margin. One or two takeaways would cover a lot of the per-play gap on defense, as they did in September.

waysToLose.title: Rams pick apart the underneath
waysToLose.body: The Rams' line allows the lowest pressure rate in the league, which blunts the Raiders' best defensive trait. McVay's quick game then attacks the league's worst short-pass defense and a missed-tackle problem. Long, efficient drives that end in touchdowns inside the 20 are how this gets away.

waysToLose.title: Bowers erased, run game dead
waysToLose.body: The Rams rank first in EPA allowed to tight ends and first against deep passes. Meanwhile the Raiders' run game can't stay on schedule against anyone. If Bowers is muted and Jeanty is getting stuffed, the offense loses its two most reliable options and Cousins is forced into tight windows.

waysToLose.title: Rams ground game breaks loose
waysToLose.body: The Rams run efficiently behind a line with a top-three stuff rate. The Raiders, without Hemingway inside, allow explosive runs at the second-highest rate in the league. Chunk runs would let the Rams control the clock and keep Cousins on the sideline.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Raiders' pass rush can get home at all against the league's best pass-protecting line. If it can't, the short-pass leaks decide the game.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is the real thing and should keep the Raiders competitive almost every week. Scoring will likely dip, though, because the back of the schedule is full of top-11 defenses: Seattle, San Francisco, KC, Denver twice, Cleveland and the Chargers. The turnover pace that propped up September should fade. The run game is unlikely to improve given how badly the line is losing at the point of attack.

The flip side is that many of those same opponents have bottom-eight offenses, especially Seattle, Denver, Cleveland, the Chargers and Tennessee. That should make the defense's points-allowed line look better than its per-play numbers. Expect lower-scoring, closer games. The one-score record, now below average, has room to improve. A final record around .500 is the center of the range, and the division race is likely out of reach with KC unbeaten.
swingFactors: Whether the defense can fix its short-pass and tackling leaks without needing turnovers
Cousins staying healthy and protected against a string of strong defenses
Any life in the run game to balance the offense in close games

confidence.note: Six games split between a soft early slate and three strong opponents; new coach, but a stable QB.
